scenes.title: Toronto 1975 Incidental Memory Bench: Three 200-ms Encoding Cards ('CAPS? 17%' | 'RHYME? 48%' | 'MEANING? 82%')
scenes.era: 1972 / 1975, University of Toronto Cognitive Psychology Laboratory

layout.description: Sunlit high-key 1970s Toronto university psychology room featuring a clean oak testing desk with a 200-ms card display and Yes/No keys alongside **three tiered Stimulus Question Plaques** — **Level 1 Shallow ('Is TABLE in CAPITALS? -> 17% Recall')**, **Level 2 Phonemic ('Does CRATE rhyme with WEIGHT? -> 48% Recall')**, and **Level 3 Deep Semantic ('Does WATCH fit: She placed the ___ on the desk? -> 82% Recall')**.

positions.who: Fergus Craik & Robert Lockhart (mannequins in 1972/1975 tweed blazer, turtleneck, and collared shirt)
positions.where: sliding the three encoding-depth cards into the viewer with zero mention of a memory test, then unveiling the towering 17% -> 48% -> 82% surprise recall staircase!
positions.facing: standing beside oak desk and bar chart

positions.where: tapping 'YES' briskly to the deep sentence-fit question — then lighting up in surprise ten minutes later as 8 out of 10 deep words pop effortlessly onto their recall sheet!

props.name: three-level Encoding Question Cards (1. Font Case | 2. Rhyme Sound | 3. Sentence Meaning)
props.period_detail: identical 200-ms word flashes differed ONLY by the question asked

props.name: Surprise Recall Staircase Board ('17% Shallow -> 48% Rhyme -> 82% Deep Semantic')
props.period_detail: visualizes the nearly 5-fold memory jump without any instruction to memorize
props.physical_behavior: crystallizes Levels of Processing in one glance

actions.verb_sequence: flashes Level-1 CAPS card, Level-2 RHYME card, and Level-3 MEANING card as Participant taps Yes/No -> hands Participant an unexpected blank recall sheet -> Participant recalls almost none of the CAPS words while writing nearly every MEANING word

reactions.reaction: stares amazed at remembering words they never even tried to memorize!
point to Experiment 5 proving slow letter-counting still loses to fast meaning

scenes.wardrobe: Early-1970s Canadian academic attire: tweed jacket over turtleneck; Oxford shirt and wool cardigan.
scenes.recognition_hook: Same word, same fifth-of-a-second flash, zero warning of a test — yet asking about MEANING instead of CAPITAL LETTERS quintuples what your brain remembers!

key_visual.description: a 1975 Toronto lab desk with Yes/No keys, three encoding cards (Capitals, Rhyme, Sentence Meaning), and a steep 17%-48%-82% surprise recall bar staircase

scenes.title: Experiment 5: Slow Letter-Counting Still Loses to Fast Meaning!

layout.description: Clean desk comparing a slow 1.7-second 'C-V-C-C-V Pattern?' card (~25% recall) against a fast 0.8-second 'Sentence Meaning?' card (~80% recall).

positions.where: pointing to the stopwatch + recall inversion that crushed the 'just more time spent!' excuse

props.name: 1.7s Shallow Pattern vs 0.8s Deep Meaning comparison plaque
props.period_detail: proves conceptual elaboration — NOT raw clock seconds — drives retention

actions.verb_sequence: contrasts long letter-checking seconds (low memory) against brief meaning judgment (high memory)

reactions.reaction: see why staring longer at notes fails

scenes.recognition_hook: Spend TWICE as many seconds counting vowels and consonants and you STILL forget — half a second of real meaning wins hands down!

scenes.title: 1998 Subsequent-Memory fMRI: Predicting Recall Before the Test!

layout.description: High-key fMRI console displaying single-word brain bursts in left inferior prefrontal + parahippocampal cortex labeled 'Predicted: REMEMBERED!'.

positions.where: sorting single-trial BOLD surges during word viewing to forecast exact hits vs misses

props.name: Trial-by-Trial Subsequent Memory fMRI screen
props.period_detail: turns Craik & Lockhart's 1972 cognitive depth into visible prefrontal-hippocampal spikes

actions.verb_sequence: flags high left-PFC trials -> Volunteer recalls those exact words an hour later

reactions.reaction: amazed their recall was predicted before the quiz started

scenes.recognition_hook: Watch left prefrontal cortex light up for one second as you read a word, and fMRI can predict before the quiz whether you'll remember it tomorrow!

scenes.title: Trading Yellow Highlighters for Three 'Why?' Questions

layout.description: Tidy oak study desk where a student sets down a passive highlighter and writes one 'How does this connect to...' margin question.

positions.where: closing a heavily highlighted page (shallow) to write a 1-sentence personal analogy (deep)

props.name: Why/Analogy margin note vs passive highlighter
props.period_detail: converts Type I re-reading into Type II semantic elaboration

actions.verb_sequence: caps highlighter -> writes one concrete 'Why?' connection in 20 seconds

reactions.reaction: recalls the concept effortlessly on exam day

scenes.recognition_hook: Memory is the residue of thought — trade five passive re-reads for one genuine 'Why does this happen?' question.
